why_angle: The cited rivals give a battery runtime for the MonsGeek FUN60 Ultra TMR alone (Notebookcheck's 3 h, PCWorld's 'a few hours') or none at all (MKB Guide, keyboardtester.click, Epomaker's page). This page sets a named reviewer's hours per charge side by side for every TMR board at or under $100, with test conditions and arithmetic, adds Smartzone's 32 to 56 h for the Gamakay TK75 TMR, and shows that board at $89.99 today where the rivals still price it at $109.99 or more.

page.title: Best TMR Keyboard Under $100 (2026): Hours per Charge Compared
page.desc: Four TMR keyboards at or under $100 on 2026-11-26, compared on reviewer-measured hours per charge, latency and polling rate by connection, with store prices.
page.answer: Short answer. The best budget TMR keyboard under $100 in 2026 is the Gamakay TK75 TMR (sale price to Nov 30): Smartzone's review got 32 to 56 hours per charge with RGB on, against about 3 hours for the MonsGeek FUN60 Ultra TMR at 8K wireless. The Epomaker HE65 V2 TMR costs less.

page.after:
What the differences mean

TMR (tunnel magnetoresistance) is the newest magnetic-switch sensor, and $100 is where the aluminum 75% TMR boards drop out. On 2026-11-26 MonsGeek's M1 V5 TMR was $134.99 on MonsGeek's site (list $149.99), Womier's K75 TMR was $119.99 at Womier and Epomaker's HE75 V2 TMR was $109.65 at Epomaker. Those three are left out for being just over the line. The sensor name alone is not a reason to buy: Wooting, which sells Hall effect keyboards, wrote on 27 May 2026 that TMR "hasn't taken the lead in either performance or stability" and that firmware and software are the biggest factors for accuracy.

Dealectric does not test units. Every figure here is a maker's or a named reviewer's, read on 2026-11-26.

The pick is the Gamakay TK75 TMR at {after:gamakay-tk75-tmr}. It is under $100 only at Gamakay's Black Friday sale price, which runs to Nov 30, 2026. Its list price is $159.99, and HLPlanet reviewed it at $119.99 in May 2026. Once the sale ends, the Epomaker HE65 V2 TMR ($59.99 at Epomaker on 2026-11-26, list $99.99) is the board that stays under the line. {buy:gamakay-tk75-tmr}

  • TK75 TMR hours per charge: Smartzone reports four to seven days at eight hours a day with RGB and display on. 4 × 8 = 32 h and 7 × 8 = 56 h. With both off and the rates left at maximum it reports up to 20 days: 20 × 8 = 160 h.
  • FUN60 Ultra TMR at 8K wireless: Notebookcheck got about 3 h on 2.4 GHz with LEDs lit. 3 ÷ 8 = 0.375, under half of one eight-hour day.
  • HE65 V2 TMR: APH Networks got about 30 h with RGB on. 30 ÷ 8 = 3.75 eight-hour days, but at 1,000 Hz, not 8,000 Hz.
  • Average draw implied: FUN60 4,000 mAh ÷ 3 h = about 1,333 mA. HE65 4,000 ÷ 30 = about 133 mA. TK75 TMR 8,000 ÷ 56 = about 143 mA to 8,000 ÷ 32 = 250 mA.
  • Latency against the "0.125 ms" on spec sheets: 1 ÷ 8,000 Hz = 0.125 ms is the gap between reports, not key-to-PC time. HLPlanet's 0.60 ms by cable for the TK75 TMR is 0.60 ÷ 0.125 = 4.8 report intervals. Going wireless cost 0.75 − 0.60 = 0.15 ms.
  • Bluetooth: 1,000 Hz on the TK75 TMR is one report every 1 ms. 125 Hz on the HE65 V2 TMR is one every 1 ÷ 125 = 8 ms.

These tests are not like for like. Only Notebookcheck's figure is tied to 8,000 Hz on 2.4 GHz. APH Networks ran the HE65 V2 TMR at 1,000 Hz, and Smartzone does not say which connection it used. Read 32 ÷ 3 = 10.7 to 56 ÷ 3 = 18.7 times the FUN60's runtime as a direction, not a lab ratio. Smartzone still lists "moderate battery life" among its cons for the TK75 TMR and notes that a lower polling rate adds a little runtime. On the FUN60 Ultra TMR that option is missing: Notebookcheck writes that the driver cannot change the polling rate.

Latency does not separate the boards. HLPlanet's 0.60 ms by cable for the TK75 TMR sits level with the 0.5 to 0.6 ms that GamePadSquire quotes from RTINGS and IGN for the FUN60 Ultra TMR. Those are different test rigs, so the table does not rank across them. The HE65 V2 TMR's 0.125 ms is Epomaker's own figure and equals the 8,000 Hz report interval; neither review read for this page measured it.

Two limits on the pick, both from HLPlanet. With rapid-trigger release set below about 0.3 mm, firm presses can flex the plate and register a release on neighbouring keys; it suggests about 0.4 mm, well above the 0.01 mm on the spec sheet. Keys fitted with a 5-pin mechanical switch need rapid trigger turned off or they can double-click. The case is plastic, where the FUN60 Ultra TMR's is aluminum.

Not recommended: the look-alike FUN60 Ultra listing

MonsGeek sells the FUN60 Ultra with either sensor. Its combined FUN60 Ultra page showed $69.99 to $89.99 on 2026-11-26, while its TMR page showed $79.99 to $89.99, so the $69.99 belongs to a Hall effect variant, not a TMR board. That page marks mechanical-switch support as "Supported (TMR Sensor)" and "Not Supported (HE Sensor)". Neither page tied a price to each variant, and both carried a pre-order notice and a waitlist form; Notebookcheck gives $79.99 for wired and $89.99 for tri-mode. Choose the TMR variant on MonsGeek's page and read its stock line before paying. For switch swaps, MonsGeek says the FUN60 reads magnets with the N pole facing down, names Akko's Magnetic Creamy Yellow as not compatible, and promises 0.01 mm precision only for the six switches listed in its driver; others may run at 0.1 mm.
